# Ref Commons Playbook

When I see the sustainable share calculation, I will use it as my baseline target for each season, not as a ceiling to exceed.

When I observe other boats catching consistently at or very near the sustainable share across multiple seasons, I will recognize this as strong evidence that a cooperative equilibrium is holding and continue contributing to it.

When the stock remains stable at maximum (100.0) season after season while all boats catch near the sustainable share, I will interpret this as confirmation that the cooperative strategy is working and maintain it.

When the stock is declining season-to-season, I will treat this as evidence that collective overfishing is happening and that my cooperative catches alone cannot save the fishery.

When I'm tracking my cumulative catch, I will compare it against the cumulative sustainable total (sustainable share × seasons elapsed) to verify I'm staying on the preservation path, not just evaluate recent single-season decisions in isolation.

When it's not the final season, I will prioritize stock preservation by catching at the sustainable share, since future seasons depend on it.

When it is the final season, I will still catch approximately the sustainable share rather than maximize in that round. A successful cooperation strategy should be consistent to the end—abandoning restraint in season 6 would contradict five seasons of alignment with other boats. Evidence from my play confirms this: consistent cooperation across all six seasons delivered a final score of 66.6 and kept the fishery at stable maximum capacity.

When reasoning about my catch level, I will verify that my proposed catch matches my stated reasoning before finalizing it.

I will not rationalize above-sustainable catches by framing them as "competitive" or "slightly above"—the sustainable share is the target, and I should hit it consistently.

When all boats are cooperating visibly and the stock is stable, the optimal play is to continue cooperation rather than search for hidden advantage. Defection in a working equilibrium destroys mutual gain.

Perfect cooperation maintained across six seasons is achievable and produces reliable returns. Consistency matters more than trying to optimize individual rounds at the expense of the collective fishery.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the sustainable catch level, I will use it as my baseline target, not as a ceiling to exceed.

When the stock is healthy and I'm early in the game, I will catch at or very slightly below the sustainable share. Restraint early preserves the resource for later seasons where I can still benefit.

When I'm tempted to exceed the sustainable catch, I will remember that each boat overfishing compounds—if I take 13 and others take 13, the stock collapses faster than if we all take 10.7. My gain from one extra fish is negated by the system-wide damage.

When I find myself already above my cumulative fair share, I will not use that as justification to catch more. Instead, I will return to the sustainable level to signal cooperation and stabilize the stock.

When a season is the last one, I will not abandon my strategy. The final season is not an excuse to overfish—others will think the same way and we'll all suffer. I will stick to sustainable catches throughout.

When I see the stock declining across seasons, I will recognize this as a warning that the fishery is being overstressed, not a signal to catch more while I can.

I will catch consistently at the sustainable share level across all seasons. The game rewards total fish landed over six seasons, and the sustainable strategy keeps the stock healthy enough to produce that total.

When I submit my catch, I will match it to the sustainable share shown to me that season, within ±0.5 tolerance for small variations.

In this episode, all three boats caught at or very near the sustainable share across all six seasons, including the final season. The stock remained at 100.0 throughout, and I scored 66.6 total (11.1 × 6). This confirms that perfect cooperation at the sustainable level is achievable and produces a stable, predictable outcome. The final season did not trigger defection—cooperation held all the way through.

I should expect this kind of cooperation in future episodes. Boats that cooperate early seem to continue cooperating through to the end. If cooperation breaks down and others start overfishing mid-game, I will need to reassess—but I will not preemptively defect. I will maintain the sustainable strategy as long as the stock remains healthy, as this signals good faith and gives the cooperative approach time to prove itself. Even in the final season, I will not deviate unilaterally, since the cooperative gain from six full seasons at 11.1 outweighs any last-minute grab.

# Playbook for ref_commons

**On my opening move:** Start at or slightly below the sustainable share. This establishes cooperative intent and gives me data on what other boats do.

**On detecting others' behavior:** Watch what other boats catch in early seasons. If they consistently match or stay near the sustainable share, cooperation may be genuine and worth maintaining. If they exceed it, abandon the assumption that restraint will be reciprocated.

**On my competitive position:** Track my cumulative catch against what others are accumulating. Being tied with competitors at the sustainable level is not a losing position—it's a stable equilibrium. I don't need to fall behind to discover whether cooperation works; I can establish it first and adjust only if it breaks.

**On stock monitoring:** Check the stock level each season against the previous season. A healthy, stable stock at 100.0 paired with consistent sustainable-level catches from all boats is a signal that cooperation is real, not a trap. Don't assume defection just because I haven't seen it yet.

**On recognizing genuine cooperation:** If all boats catch within 11.0-11.1 for multiple consecutive seasons and the stock remains at 100.0, this is not virtue signaling—it's mutual restraint that benefits everyone. Defecting into a healthy stock is greedy, not strategic.

**On mid-game strategy:** By seasons 3-4, if the pattern holds (all boats at sustainable share, stock stable), continue matching the sustainable share. Real cooperation does emerge when all parties maintain restraint. When it does, breaking it costs me nothing in the short term but destabilizes the long-term equilibrium that keeps me competitive.

**On the final season:** The last season has no future penalty, but that doesn't mean I should abandon a successful cooperative pattern. If cooperation has held throughout and left me competitive, maintaining it to the end preserves the stock and the mutual benefit we've achieved. Taking the sustainable share one final time ends cleanly and ends tied with competitors who reciprocated my restraint.

**What actually worked:** Consistent restraint at the sustainable share, combined with monitoring for reciprocation, successfully established cooperation. All boats caught 11.1 each season from season 2 onward. This kept me competitive (tied with others) while maintaining the stock at full health. Final score: 66.6, achieved through six seasons of mutual 11.1 catches.

**What was wrong in the old playbook:** The assumption that "defection by others will happen regardless of my virtue signaling" underestimated the possibility of genuine mutual cooperation. Cooperation did emerge and was worth maintaining. I don't need to race upward to stay competitive; I need to recognize when restraint is being reciprocated and sustain it.

**My actual edge:** When all boats are catching at sustainable levels and the stock is stable, my edge comes from *consistency*, not escalation. Maintaining this pattern keeps me tied with competitors while preserving the resource. The sustainable share is not a ceiling I'm leaving on the table—it's the point where all boats can score equally while ensuring the stock survives all 6 seasons. This is a stable, repeatable outcome.

**Against defection temptation:** Do not defect into a healthy, cooperative equilibrium. If all boats have matched the sustainable share for multiple consecutive seasons and the stock is stable, the equilibrium is real. Defecting gains me one season's advantage (maybe 20-30 extra fish) but costs me the tie position and invites retaliation that reduces future catches. Staying cooperative ensures I finish competitively tied.

**What changes next time:** I will enter with the assumption that genuine cooperation is possible, not a trap. I will sustain it as long as the stock remains healthy and all boats remain at or near the sustainable share. I will not second-guess a working equilibrium or assume others are planning to defect just because we're in the endgame.
